storm.summary_layperson: A line of thunderstorms tracking in from the west looks on course to reach the cove by roughly 8:44 PM tonight, and this time the Sound's water isn't cool enough to blunt it the way it sometimes can.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Sound water is only 2°F cooler than the air (73°F vs 75°F) — nowhere near the gap needed to build the marine layer that sometimes weakens incoming storms.
storm.detail_html:
KOKX's 7:59 PM radar scan shows an active line of showers and thunderstorms strung from due west through southwest of the cove, roughly 13–23 miles out, with echoes running 40–48 dBZ — including two cells at 21–23 miles that are already hitting 48 dBZ. The whole system is tracking east-northeast at about 25 kt (radar-centroid motion), a course that carries it toward Riverside rather than past it.

Normally the cove has a trick up its sleeve here: cool Sound water sitting under warm inland air can build a stable marine layer that chokes off low-level convection as it crosses the water. Not tonight — the water is running 73°F against 75°F air, just a 2°F gap, far short of the roughly 10°F+ delta the mechanism needs. In the fetcher's own words: "air/water are too close in temperature for the cove to behave differently than inland." There's no protective discount to apply.

With that modifier off the table, the nearest cell's radar-tracked path is the best read: it's 13.2 miles west, closing at 15.4 kt, for an ETA of 8:44 PM (window 8:33–8:55 PM), and confidence is high because the motion estimate comes straight from paired radar scans rather than a model-steering fallback. Expect Riverside to see essentially the same thunderstorm risk as Stamford, Port Chester, and the rest of the surrounding shoreline tonight — no meaningful local buffer.

The NWS Upton area forecast discussion backs this up: a very warm, humid airmass with precipitable water near 2 inches is in place, so any storms that do fire bring a heavy-downpour risk, and forecasters specifically flagged showers and thunderstorms "in the vicinity of NYC metros on N and W" this evening — exactly the quadrant now lighting up on radar. Wind shear (23–24 kt) and mid-level lapse rates are described as weak, though, so this reads as a heavy-rain-and-lightning threat rather than an organized severe-wind or hail setup. CAPE is still 0 J/kg at the cove right now but the HRRR run shows it building to 800–1050 J/kg later tonight, so a second, more unstable round is possible after this line clears — though that's past this window.

What would change the call: if the line weakens or takes a more northerly track and slides above the cove, or if the marine layer strengthens unexpectedly (unlikely given tonight's tiny air-water gap). Barring that, treat the 8:33–8:55 PM window as solid.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked storm cell 13 miles west, closing at about 15 kt with no marine layer to slow or weaken it — trust this window as given.

wind.tactics_blurb: Light, unsettled gradient wind (5–6 kt) with no sea breeze in play tonight, and RYC's cove reading is diverging sharply from the regional ensemble — a sign of local eddying, not a pattern worth playing. The bigger story is a radar-tracked storm cell closing from the west with an ETA near 8:44 PM: expect a squally interruption in that window, so stay flexible and watch for a start delay rather than committing to either side of the course.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Tonight is a gradient-wind evening, not a sea-breeze day — even though one ingredient is present. The sea-breeze fraction across coastal stations is 0.43 (0.0 inland), building but the air–water temperature difference is only 2.2°F, well short of the roughly 5°F gate the thermal mechanism needs to organize. With that gate unmet, this classifies as gradient-only, and the regional airport-anemometer mean of 5.6 kt lands it on the light end (light gradient is under 8 kt).

There's no clean geographic driver to favor one side of the course. RYC itself is reading E (90°) at just 4.3 kt (10-min average only 2.7 kt), while the broader station ensemble median sits at SSE (151°) — a roughly 60° split, and direction agreement across the network is only 0.48, well below the 0.7 threshold that would suggest a coherent regional flow. That combination points to local eddying right at the cove rather than a signal worth racing off of; favor the center of the course and play what you actually see rather than committing to a side.

HRRR's own hourly output shows a similarly unsettled picture: SE (133°) at the top of the window, backing briefly to ESE (108°) by 21:00, then SE (125°) again by 22:00 — a wander rather than a trend, consistent with the low direction agreement. Current obs (ESE, 119°) sit only 14° off the HRRR forecast direction, a small enough gap that no correction is warranted (this isn't a sea-breeze day, so the maturation-correction logic doesn't apply anyway).

The bigger factor for this window isn't the ambient gradient at all — it's the radar-tracked thunderstorm cell closing on the cove from the west, with an ETA around 8:44 PM (see the storm section). Expect the ambient 5–6 kt drift to be briefly overridden by gusty, shifting outflow winds as that cell passes, roughly 8:30–9:00 PM, before returning to light and variable. Fleets should expect a low-pressure, drifter-class evening bracketed by a squally interruption — race committees should watch that window closely and be ready to hold or postpone starts around it.
